title: I like it — and the sentence that turns itself around
goal: Talk about likes, hobbies, and free time — using a sentence pattern that swaps subject and object compared with English.
bekal: use the dative forms: мне, тебе, ему, ей, нам, вам, им
say whether something suits you or not
build feeling sentences with no subject: мне холодно, мне скучно

dialogs.title: Диалог — Weekend plans
dialogs.intro: Даша invites Ani out. Watch how нравится works: the subject of the sentence isn't the person who likes, but the thing that is liked.

notes: **Нравиться turns the sentence around.** ⚠️ *Мне нравится Москва* literally means "to me Moscow is pleasing." The **subject of the sentence is Moscow**, not me — and that's why the verb agrees with Moscow, not with me. If the thing liked is plural, the verb goes plural: *Мне нравя**тся** музеи*. English speakers almost always try *Я нравлюсь Москва*, which means something very different ("I am pleasing to Moscow").

**Любить vs. нравиться — both mean "like," but they're not interchangeable.** Rule of thumb: **любить** for lasting, general preferences (*Я люблю кофе* — I like coffee, always). **Нравиться** for an impression of something specific, often new (*Мне нравится этот кофе* — this coffee is good). For people, любить is much stronger; *Ты мне нравишься* means "I like you / I'm into you," while *Я тебя люблю* means "I love you."

**The dative is "to whom."** Мне, тебе, ему, ей, нам, вам, им. You already used it in Unit 7 for age (*Мне двадцать лет*), and now for likes. This case is used whenever something is **directed to** someone: given, liked, felt, or said.
**Никому не нравится — a double negative again.** Literally "to nobody is not pleasing." The same pattern as никогда не and ничего не in Unit 6.

**Мне холодно, мне скучно, мне больно — feelings with no subject.** ⚠️ Compare *Холодно* (it's cold, the weather) with *Мне холодно* (I'm cold). Adding the dative moves the feeling onto someone. This pattern is very Russian: not "I am cold" but "to me it's cold."

**Кататься на коньках / на лыжах / на велосипеде** — to ice-skate / to ski / to ride a bike. The verb кататься itself means "to glide, to ride for fun," and the equipment is named with **на + prepositional**.
**Понравится is the perfective form of нравиться, and it means "will like."** *Тебе понравится* — you'll love it. A very common phrase for convincing someone.

grammars.title: The dative — to whom
body: The form used for the receiver: the one who is given something, who likes, who feels, who is a certain age.
after: For nouns, the dative singular ending: masculine & neuter → **-у/-ю** (брат → брату), feminine → **-е** (сестра → сестре, мама → маме).
⚠️ The feminine **-е** ending is exactly the same as the prepositional. One ending, two cases — a rare bit of economy from Russian.

grammars.title: Нравиться — match the verb to the thing LIKED
body: This is the key to the whole unit. The verb form depends on the thing liked, not the person who likes it.
after: ⚠️ Never change **мне** because the thing changes. Мне stays мне; the verb is what changes. The most common mistake: *Мне нравятся Москва* (wrong — Moscow is singular, so нравится).

blocks.title: Играть в or играть на ⚠️
items: **играть В + accusative** for games and sports: *играть в футбол*, *играть в шахматы* (chess), *играть в карты* (cards).
**играть НА + prepositional** for musical instruments: *играть на гитаре*, *играть на пианино*, *играть на скрипке* (violin).
This split is strict and can't be swapped. English also says "play soccer" but "play *the* guitar" — use that as your memory hook: no "the" → в, "the" → на.

blocks.text: The pattern **dative + adverb** says how something feels to someone. There's no verb at all in the present tense.

head: Русский
Say it
English
rows: It's all the same to me, I don't mind.

blocks.text: In the past add **было**, in the future add **будет**: *Мне **было** холодно* (I was cold), *Мне **будет** трудно* (it will be hard for me). The form is always neuter and never changes.
